title: The state that forgot to mention it was doing the energy transition — Eddie Would Go

G E O P O L I T I C S  .  E N E R G Y  .  U N I T E D  S T A T E S  .  19 min read
u.El estado que se olvidó de avisar que ha: The state that forgot to mention it was doing the energy transition.
u.\"¿Odiás tanto las renovables como para: "Do you hate renewables so much that you would take down the Texas economy with them?"
u.- Doug Lewin, consultor del grid eléctri: - Doug Lewin, Texas electricity grid consultant, 2025
u.Hay una narrativa que domina el debate e: There is a narrative that has dominated the global energy debate for fifteen years. It goes more or less like this: the transition to renewable energy is a left-wing project, driven by European regulators, climate activists and California Democrats. Conservative states, the ones with oil beneath their feet and cowboys in their founding myths, are on the other side. They are the ones who slow it down, who deny it, who keep the coal plants running while the world changes.
Texas did not read that script.
u.El estado más republicano del sur de Est: The most Republican state in the American south, the country's largest producer of oil and gas, the one with independence as a supreme value written into its cultural constitution - that state quietly built the largest clean energy infrastructure in the Western Hemisphere outside China. It did not do it with federal mandates. It did not do it with green rhetoric. It did it with free markets, cheap land, wind that never stops and sun that flattens you. And also with a pragmatism that does not let fundamentalist discourse get in the way of development strategy.
u.La paradoja texana es la historia energé: The Texan paradox is the most important energy story nobody is telling. And when it is told properly, it destroys two narratives that dominate public conversation at the same time: that the energy transition is left-wing ideology, and that fossil fuel states cannot lead on clean energy.
u.Los números que reescriben el mapa: The numbers that redraw the map
u.Al cierre del primer trimestre de 2026,: At the close of the first quarter of 2026, Texas has 96.4 gigawatts of installed clean energy capacity. That is more than a quarter of all clean capacity in the United States. It is the first state in the country's history to approach 100 GW - a threshold no other state has on its immediate horizon. California, in second place, has 46.4 GW. Oklahoma, third, has barely 15 GW.
u.Para que los números cobren dimensión ge: For those numbers to take on geopolitical dimension, the global comparison is worth making. Australia - an entire continent, 26 million inhabitants, decades of aggressive energy policy - has 45 GW of installed solar. Texas beats it. Brazil, the largest Latin American economy with 215 million people and some of the best solar resources on the planet, has 54 GW of solar. Texas matches it. South Korea, one of the most technologically advanced economies in the world, has around 25 GW of solar. Texas doubles that number.
u.Alemania, la referencia europea de la tr: Germany, the European benchmark for the energy transition, has 210 GW of total renewable capacity. It is a country of 84 million people with a state energy policy, massive subsidies and an institutional culture built around the Energiewende since the 1990s. Texas, with 30 million inhabitants and no federal energy policy obliging it to do anything, is on its way to 100 GW.
u.En viento, Texas es el líder indiscutido: In wind, Texas is the undisputed leader of the United States. It generates 28% of all the country's wind energy - almost triple the second-placed state. In solar, in 2025 it overtook California for the first time in utility-scale generation: 58,634 GWh against 53,713. In battery storage, the number is the most revealing of all: since 2019 it has multiplied its capacity by 5,500%. It begins 2026 with 13.9 GW of large-scale battery storage - and plans to reach 37 GW by the end of 2027.
u.El dato de las baterías merece detenerse: The battery figure is worth pausing on. Storage is the historic Achilles heel of renewables - the reason their critics always said that sun and wind cannot sustain a modern grid. Texas is solving that problem faster than anywhere else in the world outside China and California. And it is doing so without anyone asking it to.
u.El punto de partida de la historia texan: The starting point of the Texan story is not climate activism. It is the most improbable deregulator in American energy history: George W. Bush.
u.En 1999, cuando era gobernador de Texas,: In 1999, when he was governor of Texas, Bush signed a law that deregulated the state's electricity market and set the first renewable energy targets. He did not do it because he was worried about climate change. He did it because he wanted competitive markets and because wind energy in the Texas panhandle was already brutally cheap. Rick Perry, his successor and later Trump's energy secretary - the same man who said he wanted to abolish the Department of Energy before ending up in charge of it - continued the policy and signed off on the massive expansion of the Texan wind transmission network in 2005.
u.El resultado fue ERCOT: el Electric Reli: The result was ERCOT: the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, the independent electricity grid that covers 90% of the state and operates disconnected from the rest of the US networks. That disconnection - which in the winter of 2021 proved a catastrophic vulnerability when millions of Texans lost power - is at the same time the reason Texas was able to build its renewable system at a speed no other jurisdiction matched.
u.Vale la pena detenerse en Uri, porque la: Uri is worth pausing on, because public memory remembers it badly. In February 2021, ERCOT ordered 20,000 megawatts of rolling blackouts - the largest manually controlled outage in United States history - and more than 4.5 million Texans lost power, some for four days. The University of Texas counted at least 57 confirmed deaths; later journalistic estimates put the figure in the hundreds. Governor Abbott went out and publicly blamed frozen wind turbines. ERCOT's data later said something different: Texan natural gas production fell by almost 50% because wells, compressors and pipelines froze without having been weatherised, and gas accounts for 46% of the grid's fuel. No generation source - gas, coal, nuclear, wind - was exempt from failures that week. The real cause was the lack of investment in resilience against extreme cold, not the technology. Five years later, in January 2026, a storm of comparable magnitude met a different grid: it held, and Abbott attributed that to the new weatherisation rules required after the tragedy. The lesson Texas took five years and dozens of deaths to learn is the same one underlying the whole paradox: ideology explains badly what happened to the Texan grid. The data, sooner or later, corrects it.
u.La lógica es brutal y simple: solar y eó: The logic is brutal and simple: utility-scale solar and wind in Texas reach levelised costs of between 38 and 78 dollars per megawatt-hour. Combined cycle natural gas generation runs between 48 and 109 dollars. Wind and sun are, in Texas, the cheapest electricity available. No ideological argument beats that cost spread when a private developer's objective is to maximise returns.
u.Entre 2000 y 2025, ERCOT agregó casi 98: Between 2000 and 2025, ERCOT added almost 98 GW of new capacity. Seventy per cent - 69 GW - came from wind and solar. Not because the state demanded it. Because the market chose it. Six of the ten leading renewable states in the US voted Republican in 2024. They are the country's red belt. They are also the heart of the American energy transition.
u.El problema que Texas creó siendo tan ex: The problem Texas created by being so successful
u.En noviembre de 2025, ERCOT publicó un n: In November 2025, ERCOT published a number that shook the global energy industry: 226 gigawatts of large load interconnection requests. Texas's all-time peak demand record was 85.5 GW in August 2023. Companies are asking to connect loads equivalent to 2.6 times that record. Seventy-three per cent of those requests come from data centres.
u.Texas se convirtió en el destino de la i: Texas became the destination for artificial intelligence infrastructure for the same reasons it became a renewables leader: cheap land, lax regulation, a competitive electricity market, and the ability to build fast. Microsoft, Google, Meta, Amazon - all have or have announced giga-projects in Texas. The EIA projects that electricity demand in ERCOT will grow 14% in 2026 - the largest growth of any US grid operator, by a wide margin.
u.Eso crea una tensión estructural que def: That creates a structural tension that defines the state's energy future. Data centres need electricity 24/7, reliable, without interruption. Renewables are intermittent by nature - the sun does not shine at night, the wind does not always blow. The solution is batteries and natural gas as backup. Texas is building both simultaneously. In the first three months of 2026, natural gas accounted for 33% of ERCOT generation. The EIA projects that gas generation in the region will grow 7% in 2026 and another 18% in 2027.
u.La paradoja se profundiza: el estado que: The paradox deepens: the state leading the construction of renewables is also building more natural gas to sustain them. It is not incoherence - it is the logic of a transition nobody is coordinating from above and that the market resolves with whatever it has available.
u.La guerra civil republicana sobre el fut: The Republican civil war over the future of Texas
u.Y entonces llegó la política a complicar: And then politics arrived to complicate what the market was doing well.
u.En 2025, una facción del Partido Republi: In 2025, a faction of the Texas Republican Party, fed by donors tied to the fossil fuel industry and by the ideology of Project 2025 - the American right's governing manual, which called for eliminating all federal support for green energy - tried to dismantle the renewable ecosystem Texan Republicans had built over twenty-five years.
u.La ofensiva no se quedó en el Capitolio: The offensive did not stay in the state Capitol. On 4 July 2025, Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which set an expiry date on the federal tax credits that sustain much of wind and solar construction: any project that does not begin construction before 4 July 2026 - or that does not enter operation before 31 December 2027 - loses the Investment Tax Credit and the Production Tax Credit in force since the Obama era. Three days later, an executive order instructed the Treasury to "strictly enforce" that cut-off and to prevent developers from massaging the construction start date to dodge it. It is the most serious attack the Texan renewable ecosystem has suffered since its birth, and it comes, once again, from Washington and not from the market. But it has a crack that says a great deal about the real priorities behind the law: battery storage is exempt. The storage ITC does not expire in 2026 or in 2027. While the administration puts a stopwatch on wind and solar, it leaves untouched the subsidy for the technology Texas needs so that data centres do not lose power at night. It is not a minor contradiction: it is proof that even those who make the most noise against renewables understand that without batteries the grid cannot carry the demand they themselves attracted.
u.La respuesta vino de donde menos se espe: The response came from where it was least expected: from rural Republicans themselves. A Texan rancher who leases his land to wind developers put it with a clarity no political speech can match: you used to curse the wind. Now you pray for it to keep blowing. In Texas, rural communities - the most Republican in the state - depend on renewable lease income to fund schools, hospitals and infrastructure. Wind and sun are, for those communities, what oil was for the previous generation: a rent from the subsoil.
u.Doug Lewin - presidente de Stoic Energy: Doug Lewin - president of Stoic Energy and author of the most widely cited newsletter on the ERCOT grid in the Texan press - said it to The New York Times in May 2025, in the middle of the legislative debate over forcing renewables to pay for their own round-the-clock backup, with the cruelty of someone who knows the numbers: "Do you hate renewables so much that you would take down the Texas economy with them?" It is not a rhetorical question. It is the synthesis of the dilemma facing the Texan Republican Party: between the ideology they imported from Washington and the economic pragmatism that built the state they govern.
u.Por ahora, el mercado está ganando. En 2: For now, the market is winning. In 2026, Texas accounts for 40% of all new utility-scale solar capacity in the US and 53% of all new battery capacity. Tehuacana Creek 1 - 837 megawatts of solar plus 418 MW of storage - is the largest solar project entering operation in the US this year. It is in Texas.
u.Lo que Texas le dice al mundo: What Texas is telling the world
u.Hay una lección geopolítica en la histor: There is a geopolitical lesson in the Texan story that goes beyond the gigawatts installed.
u.La narrativa dominante sobre la transici: The dominant narrative about the energy transition presents it as a project imposed from above: international agreements, state regulation, government subsidies, social pressure. Texas refutes that narrative empirically. The fastest and most massive transition in the Western Hemisphere happened in the most anti-regulatory state of the country most reluctant to make international climate commitments. Not because anyone ordered it. Because it was good business.
u.Eso tiene implicancias para América Lati: That has implications for Latin America. Argentina has more sun than Texas. Chile has more wind. Brazil has both, and water besides. The resources are there. What has historically been missing are the market conditions that make investment profitable. The Texan case demonstrates that when those conditions exist - cheap land, agile permitting, energy prices set by the market, growing demand - private capital makes the transition without anyone forcing it to.
u.La segunda lección es sobre el rol de la: The second lesson is about the role of demand. Texas did not build 96 GW of clean energy to meet climate targets. It built it because it needs electricity. Artificial intelligence, data centres, crypto mining, industrial electrification - that new and voracious demand was the real engine of renewable investment. Climate change did not convince Texan investors. Microsoft's data centre electricity bill did.
u.La tercera lección es sobre las contradi: The third lesson is about the contradictions every real transition produces. Texas leads in renewables and leads in oil simultaneously. It builds batteries and builds gas plants at the same time. Its political leaders publicly attack green energy while its markets expand it at record speed. There is no narrative coherence in that story. There is, instead, a truth about how the world changes: not in an orderly or ideologically consistent way, but through economic forces that impose themselves on the discourse.
u.El estado que no pidió permiso: The state that did not ask permission
u.En abril de 2026, ERCOT proyectó que la: In April 2026, ERCOT projected that summer peak demand could reach 98,000 MW - almost double the record of three years ago. To meet that demand, it has more than 195 GW of new capacity in the development queue. Most of it is solar and batteries.
u.Ningún acuerdo internacional lo requirió: No international agreement required it. No federal mandate ordered it. No governor promised it on the campaign trail. The Texas electricity market, designed by Republicans to be the freest in the country, produced the most accelerated energy transition in the Western Hemisphere.
u.Texas no pidió permiso para hacer la tra: Texas did not ask permission to make the transition. It made it.
u.Eso debería hacernos pensar en qué narra: That should make us think about which narratives about energy we take as true, and which are simply comfortable stories that do not survive contact with the data.
